column1: A0|pronunciation|Alphabet names|Letter names help spell words; their sounds within words depend on context.|Comment ça s'écrit ?|How is that spelled?
A0|pronunciation|Accents|Accents can affect pronunciation or distinguish written words.|Où est le café ?|Where is the café?
A0|pronunciation|Silent endings|Many final consonants are silent, with exceptions and liaison.|Le chat est grand.|The cat is big.
A0|pronunciation|Elision|Le, la, je, and ne often lose their vowel before a vowel or mute h.|J'aime l'école.|I like school.
A0|pronunciation|Nasal vowels|In many contexts an or en, on, and in represent nasal vowels.|Un bon pain.|A good loaf of bread.
A0|pronunciation|Liaison|Some normally silent final consonants link to the next vowel-initial word.|Nous avons un ami.|We have a friend.
A1|grammar|Subject pronouns|French finite verbs normally need an explicit subject.|Elle parle français.|She speaks French.
A1|grammar|Tu and vous|Tu is informal singular; vous is formal singular or plural.|Vous parlez français ?|Do you speak French?
A1|grammar|Gender|Nouns have grammatical gender; learn each noun with its article.|Une maison et un jardin.|A house and a garden.
A1|grammar|Plural nouns|Most written plurals add s, though it is often silent.|Les livres sont ici.|The books are here.
A1|grammar|Definite articles|Le, la, l', and les identify specific or generic referents.|J'aime le café.|I like coffee.
A1|grammar|Partitives|Du, de la, de l', and des can indicate an unspecified quantity.|Je bois de l'eau.|I drink water.
A1|grammar|Contractions|À plus le becomes au; de plus les becomes des.|Je vais au marché.|I am going to the market.
A1|grammar|Present -er verbs|Most regular -er verbs take e, es, e, ons, ez, ent in the present.|Nous parlons français.|We speak French.
A1|grammar|Basic negation|In careful writing ne precedes the verb and pas follows it.|Je ne sais pas.|I do not know.
A1|grammar|Questions|Use intonation, est-ce que, or inversion according to register.|Est-ce que tu viens ?|Are you coming?
A1|grammar|Possessive determiners|Possessives agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner's gender.|Marie cherche son livre.|Marie is looking for her book.
A1|grammar|Adjective agreement|Many adjectives change spelling with feminine and plural nouns.|Les grandes maisons sont belles.|The big houses are beautiful.
A1|grammar|Adjective position|Many descriptive adjectives follow nouns; a common group precedes them, and position can change meaning.|Une belle maison est ici.|A beautiful house is here.
A1|grammar|Imperative basics|Commands normally omit the subject pronoun.|Parlez plus lentement.|Speak more slowly.
A2|grammar|Present -ir verbs|Finir and similar verbs use -iss- in the present plural.|Nous finissons bientôt.|We are finishing soon.
A2|grammar|Present -re verbs|Many -re verbs have singular endings s, s, nothing; forms vary by verb.|Nous attendons le bus.|We are waiting for the bus.
A2|grammar|Reflexive pronouns|Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject.|Elle se lève tôt.|She gets up early.
A2|grammar|Passé composé|A completed past event typically uses present avoir or être plus a past participle.|J'ai fini mon travail.|I finished my work.
A2|grammar|Être agreement|With être, the past participle generally agrees with the subject.|Elles sont arrivées.|They arrived.
A2|grammar|Imparfait|Use the imperfect for habitual or background past events.|Quand j'étais petit, je lisais beaucoup.|When I was little, I read a lot.
A2|grammar|Near future|Aller in the present plus infinitive expresses a planned near future.|Je vais partir.|I am going to leave.
A2|grammar|Simple future|The future commonly adds ai, as, a, ons, ez, ont to its stem.|Nous partirons demain.|We will leave tomorrow.
A2|grammar|Direct object pronouns|Le, la, and les replace direct objects and usually precede the finite verb.|Je la vois.|I see her.
A2|grammar|Indirect object pronouns|Lui and leur replace some à plus person complements.|Je leur téléphone.|I call them.
A2|grammar|Demonstratives|Ce, cet, cette, and ces point to a noun.|Cet hôtel est grand.|This hotel is big.
A2|grammar|Y and en|Y often replaces a place or à phrase; en often replaces a de phrase or quantity.|J'en prends deux.|I will take two of them.
A2|grammar|Negative quantity|After many negations, an indefinite or partitive article becomes de.|Je n'ai pas de pain.|I do not have any bread.
B1|grammar|Relative qui and que|Qui is subject of its clause; que is direct object.|Le livre que je lis est long.|The book I am reading is long.
B1|grammar|Relative où|Où can refer to a place or time.|Le jour où je suis arrivé était froid.|The day I arrived was cold.
B1|grammar|Conditional present|Use conditional forms for politeness, hypotheses, and imagined results.|Je voudrais partir.|I would like to leave.
B1|grammar|Si with imperfect|Si plus imperfect often pairs with present conditional for an unreal present condition.|Si j'avais le temps, je viendrais.|If I had time, I would come.
B1|grammar|Subjunctive trigger|Certain wishes, emotions, doubts, and impersonal expressions call for subjunctive.|Il faut qu'elle vienne.|She has to come.
B1|grammar|Infinitive alternative|When the subjects are the same, many expressions use an infinitive instead of que plus subjunctive.|Je veux partir.|I want to leave.
B1|grammar|Passive voice|Être plus past participle can place focus on the event or recipient.|La route est fermée.|The road is closed.
B1|grammar|Restricted ne...que|Ne...que means only; it is not a simple negative.|Je n'ai que deux euros.|I only have two euros.
B1|grammar|Reported speech|Que introduces many reported statements; tense may shift after a past reporting verb.|Elle a dit qu'elle était prête.|She said that she was ready.
B1|grammar|Adverbs and connectors|Connectors signal addition, opposition, result, and sequence.|Pourtant, il est parti.|Nevertheless, he left.
B2|grammar|Plus-que-parfait|The pluperfect places an event before another past event.|J'avais fini avant son arrivée.|I had finished before her arrival.
B2|grammar|Conditional past|A past conditional can describe an unreal result or unconfirmed report.|J'aurais aimé venir.|I would have liked to come.
B2|grammar|Past unreal si|Si plus pluperfect commonly pairs with a past conditional.|Si j'avais su, je serais venu.|If I had known, I would have come.
B2|grammar|Dont|Dont replaces many de complements in relative clauses.|L'idée dont je parle est simple.|The idea I am talking about is simple.
B2|grammar|Lequel forms|Lequel and its variants follow many prepositions; contract with à or de.|Le dossier auquel je pense est ici.|The file I am thinking of is here.
B2|grammar|Object pronoun order|When two object pronouns precede a verb, their order follows a fixed pattern.|Je le lui donne.|I give it to him or her.
B2|grammar|Past participle with avoir|With avoir, a preceding direct object can trigger participle agreement.|Les lettres que j'ai écrites sont ici.|The letters I wrote are here.
B2|grammar|Subjunctive after concession|Bien que commonly introduces a subjunctive clause.|Bien qu'il pleuve, nous sortons.|Although it is raining, we are going out.
B2|grammar|Gerund|En plus present participle can express manner or simultaneous action.|Elle apprend en lisant.|She learns by reading.
B2|grammar|Passive nuance|Passive voice can omit the agent; choose active when the actor matters.|Le rapport a été publié.|The report was published.
C1|grammar|Nominalization|Turn clauses into noun phrases selectively for concise formal prose.|La réduction des délais est urgente.|Reducing delays is urgent.
C1|grammar|Register|Choose pronouns, formulas, and syntax appropriate to audience and situation.|Je vous saurais gré de répondre.|I would be grateful if you replied.
C1|grammar|Prosody|Rhythm and intonation can signal contrast, attitude, and discourse structure.|C'est possible, mais peu probable.|It is possible, but unlikely.
C1|grammar|Past simple recognition|Passé simple is common in literary narrative; productive use depends on genre.|Il entra dans la pièce.|He entered the room.
C1|grammar|Reported conditional|The conditional may distance a writer from unverified information.|Il aurait quitté la ville.|He reportedly left the city.
C1|grammar|Expletive ne|After certain expressions, ne can appear without negative force in formal French.|Je crains qu'il ne soit trop tard.|I fear it may be too late.
C1|grammar|Pronominal participle agreement|Agreement depends on whether the reflexive pronoun is a direct or indirect object.|Elles se sont parlé.|They spoke to each other.
C1|grammar|Reformulation|A clear paraphrase can make specialized content understandable to another audience.|Autrement dit, le délai est prolongé.|In other words, the deadline is extended.
C2|communication|Implicature|Interpret what is implied by context, tone, and shared assumptions.|Il aurait pu prévenir.|He could have warned us.
C2|communication|Hedging|Modulate confidence without disguising missing evidence.|Il semble plausible que cela change.|It seems plausible that this will change.

C2|communication|Rhetorical concession|Acknowledge a valid objection before defending a qualified position.|Certes, le coût est élevé ; toutefois, le gain est durable.|Admittedly the cost is high; however, the gain is lasting.
C2|communication|Idiomatic register|Use idioms when they fit the context and audience.|Tout bien pesé, il vaut mieux attendre.|All things considered, it is better to wait.

C2|communication|Source synthesis|Retain attribution, disagreement, and limits when merging sources.|Les études convergent, mais leurs méthodes diffèrent.|The studies converge, but their methods differ.

C2|communication|Repair and precision|Rephrase promptly when a term is ambiguous or an implication is wrong.|Je reformule : il s'agit d'une option, pas d'une décision.|Let me rephrase: it is an option, not a decision.
